I listen for sounds that might mean someone is entering my home

I have lost my faith in people, life, or a higher power
I was betrayed by someone I trusted

vignette: Lieutenant Ryder Jenkins, a 32-year-old combat pilot, had always prided himself on his ability to stay focused under pressure. But everything changed one fateful night when he was sexually assaulted by a fellow officer while stationed overseas. The event left him shaken and struggling to come to terms with what had happened. At first, Ryder tried to push the memories of that night aside and focus on his work. However, he soon found himself constantly on edge, jumping at ordinary sounds like the creaking of the plane's metal or the sudden roar of the engines. He would listen intently for any unusual noises in his quarters, his heart racing with every snap or rustle. Even inside his own home, Ryder felt like he was waiting for something to happen, always on guard. As time went by, Ryder began to notice that certain situations or people triggered these feelings of unease. When someone acted suspiciously or erratically, Ryder's mind would immediately go back to that night and the sense of vulnerability it had left him with. He started to avoid social gatherings and public places, fearing he might encounter someone who would set off this chain reaction. Unpredictable situations, like turbulence during flights or unexpected changes in mission plans, also left him feeling anxious and trapped. Ryder couldn't shake the feeling that these reactions made him a "lousy coper." He had always been able to handle stress, but now he felt like he was barely holding it together. This self-doubt fueled his already heightened sense of threat, making him even more vigilant for potential dangers. Ryder became convinced that people were not what they seemed and that life was inherently unpredictable and cruel. As these negative appraisals deepened, Ryder found himself increasingly on edge, constantly monitoring his surroundings for signs of danger. He started to feel like he was walking around with a target on his back, waiting for someone to strike again. This perpetual state of alertness took a toll on his relationships and daily life, causing him to pull away from friends and family. One night, Ryder woke up from a nightmare, drenched in sweat and gasping for air. The dream residue lingered long after he woke up, leaving him feeling disoriented and frightened. He couldn't shake the image of himself as a helpless victim, unable to defend himself against an unseen attacker. This episode left Ryder feeling even more disconnected from his past self, like he had lost all sense of control. The memories of that night still haunted Ryder, but what frightened him most was the sense of betrayal that lingered long after the assault. He couldn't understand how someone he trusted could do such a thing. This feeling of betrayal seeped into every aspect of his life, making it hard for him to trust anyone or anything. It wasn't until Ryder's performance as a pilot began to suffer that he realized he needed help. His squadron commander noticed the change in him and encouraged Ryder to seek counseling. With great reluctance, Ryder finally made an appointment, hoping to find a way to break free from this cycle of fear and self-doubt that had consumed his life. As Ryder sat in the therapist's office, he knew it wouldn't be easy to confront these demons head-on. But for the first time since the assault, he felt a glimmer of hope – maybe, just maybe, he could learn to trust himself again and find a way to heal.
